active_narratives.title: Fed Rate Expectations: CPI Surprise & Pause Debate
active_narratives.summary: Debate is rate HIKES, not cuts: the Fed HELD at 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 (second under Warsh) but three officials — Hammack, Kashkari, Logan — dissented FOR a 25bp hike, the first same-direction triple dissent since September 2016, so the committee splits hawkish. July CPI (Aug 12) printed IN LINE at 3.4% YoY headline (+0.1% MoM) with core 2.5% (a '3.3%' figure is the FRED SA series). The AUGUST JOBS REPORT (BLS, Sep 4) beat hard — payrolls +162k vs ~55k consensus, July REVISED from -23k to +21k, June to +31k, unemployment 4.1%, AHE +3.1% y/y — and September pricing settled at 58.4% for a 25bp hike to 3.75-4.00% (CME FedWatch, Sep 4 close; 49.4% on Sep 3 after Governor Waller said he 'would be inclined to support holding' if the next two weeks of data cooperate, ~65% intraday post-print), with ~35bp of hikes priced by the Dec 9 meeting and no cut priced at any 2026 meeting. Warsh (Jackson Hole, Aug 28) holds the 2% line with guidance 'limited and circumscribed'. US10Y 4.78% (Sep 4; 4.79% Sep 1-2 — matched the highest since May 29, 2024, NOT 'since Jan 2025'), 2Y 4.37%, 30Y 5.24% (below its Aug 17 high of 5.30%).
active_narratives.thesis: If inflation stays sticky above target, the Fed's next move is a hike, and after the August payrolls beat the September meeting is a live coin-flip-plus rather than a Q4 story: the three hike-dissents stand, Collins (Aug 25) says it will be 'appropriate to tighten policy soon' absent sustained progress, and zero cut probability is priced at any 2026 meeting. The August CPI (Fri Sep 11, before the Sep 15-16 meeting, which carries fresh projections) is the named swing factor — sell-side consensus after the jobs print is 'hike unless CPI surprises to the downside'. Two-sided: Waller's Sep 3 conditional-hold framing is the dovish voice inside the committee, and Trump publicly demanded cuts on jobs day — political pressure, not a pricing input. Do not read any soft print as cut-risk — nothing is priced there.

active_narratives.title: Hyperscaler AI Capex Bubble Concerns: Datacenter $1.7T by 2030 vs. ROI Validation Risk
active_narratives.summary: Hyperscaler AI capex has outgrown the original $1.7T-by-2030 framing so decisively that its author retired it: Dell'Oro nearly DOUBLED its data-center capex forecast to >$3T by 2030 on Aug 18, 2026 (from $1.7T in January, newly counting the AI-specialized cloud segment). The Big Four alone guide to roughly $730B in 2026 (Alphabet $195-205B, Amazon ~$220B after raising from ~$200B on Jul 30, Microsoft $175B for CALENDAR 2026, restated from ~$190B on a useful-life reclass with spend unchanged, Meta $130-145B after narrowing from $125-145B on Jul 29 — a $5B floor raise, per the release verbatim) and analysts project ~$1T in 2027 (a circulating '$1.15T' is Morgan Stanley's figure INCLUDING SpaceX as a new hyperscaler — not like-for-like). Semiconductor supply chains benefit directly, but ROI-validation and financing-cost concerns have intensified as the numbers grew — a WSJ report (~Aug 18) put ~$3T of off-balance-sheet, mostly AI-related commitments across nine top tech firms.
active_narratives.thesis: AI infrastructure spending remains a strong tailwind for semis, memory, optics and power infrastructure, but multiple-compression risk emerges if capex growth decelerates or demand does not materialise. The Q2 2026 print season is now COMPLETE and it resolved in favour of continuation: all four reported by 30 July and none guided down — Alphabet RAISED to $195-205B on 22 July flagging a significant further increase in 2027, Meta narrowed to $130-145B (from $125-145B — a $5B floor raise) on 29 July, Microsoft restated calendar-2026 capex to $175B on a useful-life reclass (buildings 15-to-25 years, effective FY2027) with spend unchanged, and Amazon RAISED to ~$220B on 30 July. Read the Amazon raise as a different kind: it was attributed to HIGHER MEMORY COSTS — paying more for the same capacity, not buying more — so it is a weaker demand signal than a unit-driven raise and it transmits to memory vendors rather than along the whole chain, though Jassy said Amazon still will not have enough capacity for 2026 demand. The live constraint has shifted from willingness to spend toward the cost of funding it — the ~$12B El Paso datacenter bond (precisely: $12.55B of notes at a 7.5% coupon priced Jul 27 by the BlackRock-led JV holdco, BlackRock 80% / Meta 20%) and Amazon's $25B July issue (order book peaked ~$62B, final ~$41B, with an extra-yield concession — cooler than its March deal) are the anchors, and Alphabet's debut A$5.5B Kangaroo bond (Aug 19) priced its 20-year tranche near 7% — long-dated money for an AAA-class issuer now costs ~7% in AUD. Rates compound this: the Fed is priced hold-versus-hike rather than easing (Sep 16: ~58% hike (CME, Sep 4 close) / ~32-34% hold / 0% cut per CME on Sep 1 after Warsh's Aug 28 Jackson Hole keynote — was ~32% hike in mid-Aug, with the Jul-29 minutes showing 'several' favoring an immediate hike), which is a duration headwind for capex-intensive mega-caps. A first guide-down or 'digestion' framing from any major hyperscaler would be a cluster-wide thesis-break check, not a single-ticker event.

active_narratives.title: US-China Semiconductor Supply Chain Reshaping: Tariffs vs. Foundry Demand
active_narratives.summary: US-China technology restrictions continue to reshape semiconductor supply chains, but the direction is mixed rather than uniformly escalating. ASML's standing 2030 ambition is EUR 44-60B revenue set at its Nov 2024 Investor Day and never revised — though the FY26 guide midpoint (~EUR 44B) already touches its floor — and Intel's 18A is in volume production, with High-NA EUV dual-qualified on a subset of 18A layers in Oregon (High-NA-DEPENDENT high-volume manufacturing is a 2027/14A story, not a current fact). Onshoring economics support equipment and memory capex. China's materials levers are NOT all retaliation: the helium export prohibition (in force since Jul 10, open-ended) is GLOBAL in scope and driven by the Qatar supply shock — MOFCOM says on record it targets no country — while the genuine trade-war channel is the suspension cliffs: rare-earth/magnet measures lapse 2026-11-10 and Ga/Ge/antimony 2026-11-27, both snapping back by default; note the ban on dual-use exports to US MILITARY end users and the tungsten/indium/rare-earth measures of early 2025 were never suspended, so 'controls are paused' is too broad.
active_narratives.thesis: Structural supply-chain tailwinds from US-China decoupling support the onshoring complex — Intel 18A and 14A, ASML EUV, Micron's >$250B cumulative US plan through 2035 (raised from ~$200B on Jul 9, 2026) — while elevated cost of capital constrains the multiple paid for that demand. The policy picture is two-directional and the 'officials speaking vs agencies acting' rule now needs a SPLIT: on Moonshot specifically it still holds (no designation, no docket), but the distillation/model-export lane has formal instruments — OSTP's NSTM-4 directive on adversarial distillation (Apr 23, 2026) and a BIS is-informed letter requiring licences for certain frontier US model exports including API access (Jun 12, 2026) — while open-WEIGHT models remain uncontrolled. The Hong Kong emergency order lapsed Jul 14 and MOFCOM tariff-cut consultations (~$30B each way) continue. The durable read stands: weight enacted measures over statements — and the enacted list grew: Section 232 tariffs on unmanned aircraft systems (proclamation Aug 13, in force Sep 3; 100%/25% with allied caps, components 25% from Feb 9, 2027; China not named on its face) join polysilicon (15% + minimum prices from Dec 4) and the November materials cliffs, while the POLITICO-reported 'comprehensive semiconductor tariffs' (Aug 27) have NO Federal Register docket as of Sep 5 and Moonshot is negotiating a 30% revenue share with US hyperscalers (Reuters Aug 26) under blacklist threats that remain threats. On H200 exports to China the binding constraint is Beijing, not Washington — BIS has granted licences to 10+ Chinese firms but Beijing's posture is selective and NVIDIA recognizes zero China H200 revenue, excluding it from guidance entirely.

active_narratives.title: ECB Rate Hold Diverges from Fed Hawkish Pause: Euro Weakness Implication
active_narratives.summary: ECB held the deposit rate at 2.25% on Jul 23, 2026 after hiking 25bp on Jun 11 — its first hike since 2023 — with markets pricing a 25bp hike to 2.50% at the Sep 10 projection meeting (Berlin) at ~99% (98.9%, Sep 2). The divergence has INVERTED: this is a tightening bias, not an easing cycle, and while the rate-LEVEL premium persists (Fed 3.50-3.75% vs ECB 2.25%), both banks now lean the same way — so the divergence is about LEVEL and CONVICTION, not direction: the ECB is ~99% priced while the Fed is ~58% for Sep 16 (CME FedWatch, Sep 4 close; 49.4% on Sep 3 after Waller's conditional-hold remarks, ~65% intraday after the +162k August payrolls). The euro is NOT expressing the divergence cleanly: EUR/USD ~1.162 at the Sep 4 close (flat-to-firmer on the week, dipped below 1.16 on the jobs beat) with DXY 99.16 (down from 99.67 Sep 1) — the dollar's weakness was Waller and a ~3% yen surge on BOJ pricing, not euro strength.
active_narratives.thesis: The ECB is in a tightening bias, not an easing one: 25bp on Jun 11 to a 2.25% deposit rate, held on Jul 23 with some governors questioning whether more was warranted (a 'unanimous' vote characterization is unverified — drop it). July was a non-projection meeting so the bar to move was structurally higher; Sep 10 carries fresh forecasts and is the live decision, with the July FINAL HICP confirmed at 2.9% (Aug 20 fetch) and the August flash ~Aug 31 as the last major input. Energy-driven inflation is the shared driver with the Fed, so the policy-RATE gap is narrowing even as near-term direction diverges — the euro-weakness-on-divergence leg is the part of this narrative most at risk of being wrong, and it is now measurably inverted. Eurozone data keeps supporting the hike case: Q2 GDP +0.4% QoQ / +1.0% YoY CONFIRMED UNREVISED at the Aug 14 second estimate (employment +0.1% QoQ), and the August flash HICP jumped to 3.3% headline entirely on energy (+14.3%) while core EASED to 2.4% and services to 3.0% (from 3.3%) — services is the component the ECB actually watches, and it is now moving the DOVISH way, which is why a Reuters poll (Sep 3) has economists at one-and-done after Sep 10 while markets price another move by December; Nagel (Sep 1-2) called September 'clearly warranted' but was cautious beyond it. Global duration headwinds across developed markets still hold as a conclusion, but because everyone is tightening, not because the Fed is an outlier.

active_narratives.title: US-Iran Hormuz Blockade Escalation: Oil Supply Crisis Resurfaces
active_narratives.summary: US naval blockade of Iranian ports and the Hormuz disruption are INTACT as of Sep 4, 2026, and the conflict re-escalated into the biggest exchange of fire since July: US strikes on IRGC launchers on Larak Island (Aug 30) and on southern-coast air-defence, radar and mine-laying assets (Sep 1); Iranian missiles and drones at US bases in Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq, and from Sep 3 the UAE (no US casualties; Iran reports 12-18 dead including a wedding party in Sirik, under CENTCOM investigation); two Saudi-crude tankers struck in the strait (Aug 30/Sep 1). CENTCOM tally: 87 vessels redirected since Jul 14 (Sep 3; 83 on Aug 30). NAME THE METRIC: Kpler's visible commodity-vessel count is 4-9/day (Sep 1-3; 10-day average ~15 vs ~125/day pre-war; only two VLCCs all week) — but oil VOLUME is near pre-war (more than 17M bbl on Aug 31 vs a 21.6 mb/d pre-war average; ~15M bbl on Sep 2 per Vance) because CENTCOM declared the strait mine-free on Aug 27 and traffic uses the southern route. There is NO ceasefire and never was one in August (the Jun 17 memorandum's 60-day window expired Aug 17 with no deal); Bloomberg (Sep 4): 'We Are Stalled' — both sides far from formal talks and raising preconditions. Oman REJECTED Iran's bilateral strait-management corridor over service fees (Sep 3-4), so that track is dead, not dormant. Sanctions lane: Treasury's 'Operation Economic Outcast' launched Aug 24 (60+ entities, individuals and vessels across Iran, Turkiye, Hong Kong, India, UAE and Singapore; five new sectoral sanctions — digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, shipping; Bank Melli branches to close globally), with follow-on tranches Aug 28 (a UAE individual plus a Hong Kong trader) and Sep 4 (three Golden Global entities, Istanbul); the UAE's Aug 19 financial embargo on Iran stands. WTI 91.48 / Brent 96.28 at the Sep 4 close, +9.7% / +7.8% on the week (Sep 1 close 90.22, +5.2%); April peak close 112.95 (Apr 7; intraday 117.63).
active_narratives.thesis: The load-bearing tension has moved again: the premium is re-arming on PHYSICAL change, not headlines alone — mines cleared but tankers hit, coastal radar degraded, LNG cargoes shifted to ship-to-ship transfers outside the strait, Saudi exports diving (Sep 2). Do not read falling crude as the strait reopening (Sep 3 is the model case: WTI printed 89.57 on Trump's 'won't last long' remark and still CLOSED UP at 91.30), and do not read 'ceasefire expires' or 'peace deal' headlines as state changes — no operative ceasefire or deal exists. Two metrics disagree and reports must name which: vessel COUNT is ~-90% vs pre-war while barrel VOLUME is ~70-80% of pre-war. Offsets: Venezuela — Chevron ($7B pledge), ENI and GE signed deals under US oversight on Sep 2 (CONFIRMED) while the US claim on reserves remains a presidential announcement (REPORTED) — the only meaningful bearish supply leg in the window. Sell-side re-based UP: Goldman lifted 2026 Brent to $85 / WTI $79 with upside risk (Sep 4), Citi Q3 Brent $86 (Sep 3), Morgan Stanley Brent $90 Q3 to ~$100 Q4, JPMorgan $86/$80 on a reopening base case that has not arrived; EIA STEO next Sep 9. Transmission legs that still apply: logistics-cost inflation from rerouting pressures semiconductor supply chains (ASML, TSM, MU); record US diesel prices (Sep 3) feed the inflation impulse behind the Fed's hike debate at the Sep 15-16 FOMC (live odds live in fed_rate_pivot — do not carry a separate figure here). Falsifiable both ways: further strikes or a new sanctions tranche (weekly cadence so far) re-arm the premium; an ACTUAL reopening to normal transit — not a permissioned corridor — would be the first genuine supply improvement and has NOT happened.

active_narratives.title: Microsoft Azure AI Revenue Concentration: OpenAI 45% Backlog Dependency
active_narratives.summary: Microsoft's disclosed 45% OpenAI share of Azure backlog is a DECEMBER-quarter figure that has never been refreshed — do not quote it as current; the closest refresh is Hood's Q4 remark that commercial RPO grew +25% EXCLUDING OpenAI, with all sequential RPO growth from customers outside the frontier-model companies. The exclusivity unwind was TWO stages, not one late-April event: Microsoft's compute right-of-first-refusal ended Oct 28, 2025 (Microsoft blog, primary), and the residual Azure API exclusivity ended ~Apr 27, 2026 (REPORTED — trade-press convergence; GPT-5.5 appeared on Amazon Bedrock Apr 28), so OpenAI can now buy compute elsewhere. Q4 FY2026 printed Jul 29, 2026: commercial RPO $678B (+84% YoY) and Azure +43% constant currency, both ahead of the prior $627B/~40%.
active_narratives.thesis: Single-vendor concentration risk is real but has moved on two axes since this was written. With exclusivity fully unwound (ROFR Oct 2025, API exclusivity Apr 2026), the forward question is no longer lock-in but whether OpenAI-linked Azure consumption DECELERATES now that it can buy elsewhere — the cleaner read on calls is Azure growth ex-OpenAI, and the RPO-ex-OpenAI +25% disclosure is the first partial refresh of the concentration picture. Microsoft is also actively reducing the dependency with in-house MAI models — but the '89% cheaper than OpenAI' figure is Microsoft's own self-reported GPU-cost reduction for MAI-Voice-2-Flash in Dynamics 365 Contact Center ONLY, not API pricing and not portfolio-wide; do not generalize it. Capex is the swing factor: $175B FY2027 capex restated (from ~$190B — a useful-life reclass, spend unchanged, NOT a cut), with memory prices as the cost driver — a direct link to the memory-supercycle narrative, now confirmed from outside Microsoft by Amazon naming higher memory costs as the reason for its ~$200B to ~$220B raise on Jul 30. Two anchors here are stale and should not be reused: the 45% backlog share (December quarter, never refreshed) and the $1.7T-by-2030 capex figure, against Big-4 2026 guided capex of roughly $730B. US10Y is 4.64%, not 4.42%.

active_narratives.title: BigTech AI Strategy Divergence: GOOG TPU Upgrade vs MSFT/AMZN Caution
active_narratives.summary: Market differentiating BigTech AI exposure by structure rather than by any single day's rating: GOOG's in-house TPU stack, MSFT's OpenAI/Azure concentration, AMZN's capex load. Signal states across the three have churned repeatedly -- GOOG ran BUY to CAUTION to HOLD between June and late July -- so the durable content here is the structural split, not a signal triple that decays within days.
active_narratives.thesis: Divergence reflects structural AI strategy differences. GOOG benefits from owning its accelerator roadmap -- Ironwood GA, with 8th-gen Sunfish/Zebrafish only in select-customer preview and GA not until late 2027 -- and raised FY26 capex to $195-205B (NOT the '>=$180B' an earlier update recorded: $180-190B was the PRIOR guide). MSFT's OpenAI concentration is the most-cited risk but has softened -- the late-April rewrite ended cloud exclusivity and MSFT is shipping in-house models it says cut costs up to 89% -- and the 45% Azure-backlog share is a December-quarter figure never refreshed, so it should not be quoted as current. AMZN carries ~$220B FY26 capex (raised from ~$200B on 30 July, attributed to higher memory costs) against a genuine AWS reacceleration -- Q2 AWS grew 37% to $42.2B, its fastest since Q4 2021. The Jul 22-30 print window has now CLOSED and all three reported, so the June framing is superseded: the actuals show all three still raising or holding capex with none guiding down, and the divergence now runs on who funds it from operating cash and who is paying input-cost inflation for the same capacity.

active_narratives.title: FTC and States Sue Amazon Over Ad-Price Manipulation
active_narratives.summary: FTC and 22 states sued Amazon on Mon Aug 31, 2026 in W.D. Washington (2:26-cv-03097) — a Section 5 FTC Act DECEPTION/unfairness case plus state UDAP claims, NOT antitrust: Amazon told advertisers they would pay one cent above the second-highest bid but from 2019 ran an undisclosed 'soft reserve'/phantom-bidder floor, charging winners their full bid on ~80% of auctions by 2024 (Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, Display); FTC alleges >$20B of overcharges across >1M sellers/brands. Amazon called the suit 'misguided' the same day; AMZN fell ~3% (reported). Amazon's pipeline signal flipped CAUTION→HOLD the same day, but that flip was the >5%-extension entry block CLEARING at +3.1% vs the 50-day — mechanical, unrelated to the suit.
active_narratives.thesis: Regulatory overhang on Amazon's highest-margin line: a deception case on auction mechanics can force disclosure/pricing changes and refunds rather than structural remedies, so the near-term read is ad-revenue yield risk and headline risk, not a break-up threat. No procedural dates published yet (standard 21-day answer clock from service). The same-day HOLD signal was an entry-block clearance, not a pipeline verdict on the lawsuit — do not read it as 'impact priced'.
